text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) occurs when the tiny arteries in your lungs thicken and narrow, forcing the right side of your heart to work much harder to pump blood.
snippet_highlighted_words: tiny arteries in your lungs thicken and narrow, forcing the right side of your heart to work much harder to pump blood

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages, PAH often causes no symptoms at all. When symptoms do start, they are usually mild and easy to confuse with other heart or lung conditions like asthma or COPD:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during exercise or everyday tasks like climbing stairs or walking to the store
Lightheadedness or dizziness, particularly with exertion

text_blocks.snippet: As the right side of the heart becomes strained or begins to fail, more noticeable and serious symptoms develop:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema) in the ankles, legs, feet, or abdomen (due to fluid retention)
Fainting or syncopy (passing out during physical activity)
Heart palpitations or a racing, pounding heartbeat
Bluish lips or skin (cyanosis) from low oxygen levels
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness in rare, advanced cases

text_blocks.snippet: Because these warning signs develop slowly and overlap with other conditions, getting an accurate diagnosis requires specialized testing such as an echocardiogram or right heart catheterization through the American Lung Association.
If you or someone you know is experiencing these signs, tell me:

list.snippet: How long have these symptoms been happening?
What specific activities trigger the shortness of breath or dizziness?

text_blocks.snippet: I can help you prepare questions to discuss with a pulmonologist or cardiologist.
